1422.title: What you still ask
1422.howItsDone: Muslims bring their questions to an imam, a teacher or a scholar, in study circles at the mosque or one to one, and teachers often answer with the verse or hadith behind the answer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what changed in practice, the one habit that stayed, and your line: it stuck.

A hand goes up at the back of a study circle, just as everyone is reaching for their shoes. One more question. The teacher sits back down. A year of learning leaves a few of those behind: the verse that still puzzles, the ruling that never quite made sense, the question of why that nobody ever answered. After a year of pillars, schools and chains of narrators, some questions got answered. Others only got sharper. Today is for the sharp ones, not to close them, but to keep them. Questions are welcome here, and the texts themselves say why.
screen: `ONE MORE QUESTION.` → `SOME ANSWERED, SOME SHARPER.` → `QUESTIONS ARE WELCOME.`

segments.voice: First, the book is full of questions. More than once the Qur'an opens a passage with they ask thee, yas'alunaka, and then answers. They ask about the new moons, about wine and gambling, about what to spend, about orphans, about the spirit. Real questions became part of the book. Second, even a prophet asked. In the Qur'an, Ibrahim says, in paraphrase: my Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He is asked: do you not believe? Yes, he answers, but so that my heart may be at rest. A question isn't always doubt. Sometimes it's a heart wanting to settle. Third, not asking can do harm. In a hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud, a man with a head wound is told by his companions that they know of no allowance for him to skip washing. He washes, and he dies. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, hears of it, he is angry with them and says, in paraphrase: why didn't they ask, when they didn't know? The cure for not knowing is asking. The Qur'an says it too, in Pickthall's translation: "Ask the followers of the Remembrance if ye know not." Fourth, asking has manners. The same book says, in paraphrase, don't ask about things that would only trouble you if they were made plain. So ask what you need, ask someone who knows, and ask in order to act. In these texts, a question carried well is how learning keeps going.
screen: `THEY ASK THEE: QUESTIONS IN THE BOOK.` · `IBRAHIM ASKS, SO HIS HEART CAN REST.` · `THE CURE FOR NOT KNOWING IS ASKING.` · `ASKING HAS MANNERS TOO.`

segments.voice: Let one question from this year rise, the one still standing after the others have gone quiet: a verse, a ruling, a practice, or something bigger. Don't answer it; just find the words for it, the ones you'd want to read again next year. If you pray, you can set it before Allah in your own words, as a question still open.
What you still ask. The question this year left open, kept on purpose, because the texts make room for a question asked in order to learn. Today's word.
Your line: keep asking. A question asked in order to learn is welcome. Tomorrow, the scholars.

1423.title: Gratitude for the scholars
1423.howItsDone: Muslims say rahimahullah, may Allah have mercy on him, after the name of a scholar who has died, and teachers often open a lesson by naming the scholars whose books they are teaching from.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what you still ask, the question kept on purpose, and your line: keep asking.

Every answer this year had someone standing behind it. The chain of a hadith: a row of names, each one checked. The rule for praying while traveling: a jurist who weighed the reports, a student who copied his notes, a teacher who explained them to the next student. Some of them you'll never hear of. They sat with questions like the one you kept yesterday, and wrote down what they found and what they weren't sure of. Today is a thank-you to centuries of careful people, and why their care mattered.
screen: `EVERY ANSWER HAS SOMEONE BEHIND IT.` → `NAMES YOU'LL NEVER HEAR.` → `CENTURIES OF CAREFUL PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: First, someone has to stay and learn. The Qur'an says, in paraphrase, that the believers should not all go out at once: from every group, a party should stay behind to gain understanding of the religion, and teach their people when they come back. Learning is named as a job worth staying home for. Second, what the scholars inherit. In a hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase, that the scholars are the heirs of the prophets. The prophets left no gold and no silver. They left knowledge, and whoever takes it takes a large share. Third, why they were careful. The Qur'an counts among forbidden things, in paraphrase, saying about Allah what you do not know. So the scholars this year met, from Abu Hanifa and Malik to Ja'far al-Sadiq to Karimah al-Marwaziyyah teaching Bukhari's collection, weren't careful because they were fussy. Speaking for God without knowledge was a serious wrong to them. So they checked chains, argued over a single word, and wrote down where they disagreed. Fourth, what the teacher receives. In a hadith in Jami' al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet says, in paraphrase, that Allah and His angels, the people of the heavens and the earth, even the ant in its hole and the fish, send blessings on the one who teaches people good. The scholars were careful, and the texts ask that their care be remembered.
screen: `A PARTY STAYS BEHIND TO LEARN.` · `HEIRS OF THE PROPHETS.` · `CAREFUL, BECAUSE IT WAS SERIOUS.` · `EVEN THE ANT AND THE FISH.`

segments.voice: Bring back one scholar from this year, a name you remember: a jurist, a collector of hadith, a woman who taught. If you pray, you can say after the name the words Muslims use for those who have died: rahimahullah, may Allah have mercy on him, or rahimahallah for a woman. If you don't, simply hold the name, and thank that person quietly for the care they took.
Gratitude for the scholars. Thanks for the people who stayed behind to learn, checked every link, and feared saying about God what they did not know. Today's word.
Your line: they were careful. Their care is how the answers reached you. See you tomorrow.

1424.title: Gratitude for the ordinary
1424.hook: the people who taught you without a title
1424.howItsDone: Muslims say jazakallahu khayran, may Allah reward you with good, to thank someone, and in some families children learn the first words of the faith at home, long before any class.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gratitude for the scholars and their care, and your line: they were careful.

A broom leans against the wall by the door of a mosque. Somebody uses it every evening after the last prayer, and nobody thinks to ask who. Yesterday was for the scholars with names on book spines. Today is for the others. The grandmother who said bismillah before every bite until it stuck. The neighbor who showed a nervous kid where to put their shoes. The friend who answered a clumsy question about Ramadan without making anyone feel foolish. None of them had a title. Some taught more than any book.
screen: `A BROOM BY THE MOSQUE DOOR.` → `THE GRANDMOTHER, THE NEIGHBOR, THE FRIEND.` → `TEACHERS WITHOUT A TITLE.`

segments.voice: First, thanking people is part of thanking God. In a hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: whoever does not thank people has not thanked Allah. Gratitude that skips the person in front of you isn't finished. Second, the one who swept the mosque. In Sahih al-Bukhari there's a report about a Black woman, or a man, the narrator wasn't sure which, who used to sweep the mosque. One day the Prophet noticed she was gone and asked about her. She had died, and no one had told him. In Sahih Muslim's telling, people thought it a small matter. He said, in paraphrase: why didn't you tell me? Show me her grave. He went and prayed at her grave. Nobody had thought her worth a message. He thought her worth a visit. Third, the first teachers of all. The Qur'an asks for thanks to Allah and to one's parents in one breath. And it gives a line to say for them, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little." Care when you were little is teaching too, the kind no one writes down. Fourth, the untitled teachers now. The aunt who corrected a verse gently. The coworker who covered a shift so someone could make Friday prayer. The stranger in a mosque who lent a prayer mat and said nothing. The hadith puts thanks to them inside thanks to Allah, and the Prophet's walk to a grave shows the honor doesn't end when they do.
screen: `THANK PEOPLE, AND YOU'VE THANKED GOD.` · `THE ONE WHO SWEPT THE MOSQUE.` · `PARENTS: THE FIRST TEACHERS.` · `THANKS BELONGS TO THEM TOO.`

segments.voice: Let one face come to mind, someone who taught you something about faith, or about being a decent person, and never got called a teacher for it. Remember the moment, and shape one sentence of thanks you could give them. If they have died, and if you pray, you can say the Qur'an's line for parents, or simply ask mercy for them.
Gratitude for the ordinary. Thanks owed to the people with no title who taught by doing, because thanking them is part of thanking God. Today's word.
Your line: untitled teachers. Some of the best teaching never came with a title. Go gently.

1425.title: Humility after learning
1425.hook: and above every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing (12:76)
1425.howItsDone: Muslim scholars and teachers end a ruling or an answer with Allahu a'lam, Allah knows best, and students are taught to say I don't know rather than guess about the religion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gratitude for the ordinary, the teachers who never had a title. Your line: untitled teachers.

"And over every lord of knowledge there is one more knowing." That's half a verse of the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, and it turns up in the middle of a family drama. Yusuf, now powerful in Egypt, has had a royal cup hidden in his brother's bag, so that he can keep him close. The plan works. And right there, the verse says the plan was Allah's doing for Yusuf, then steps back and adds: there is always someone who knows more.
screen: `OVER EVERY LORD OF KNOWLEDGE…` → `YUSUF, THE CUP, THE BROTHER'S BAG.` → `ONE MORE KNOWING.`

segments.voice: First, the verse itself. Its full line says that Allah raises by degrees whom He will, and then: over every lord of knowledge there is one more knowing. Knowledge is real, and it lifts people. It also never reaches a top shelf a human can stand on. Second, a prophet learns it. Five days ago, Musa set out for the meeting of the two seas. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells how that journey began. Musa is asked who is the most learned of people, and he answers: I am. Allah reproaches him, in the hadith's telling, because he did not refer the knowledge back to Allah, and tells him of a servant who knows more. In the Qur'an Musa asks that servant, in paraphrase: may I follow you, so that you teach me some of the right guidance you were taught? A prophet becomes a student again. Third, even the angels say it. When Adam is taught the names, the angels answer, in paraphrase: glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Fourth, the words people use. Muslim teachers may close an answer with Allahu a'lam, Allah knows best. And a story people tell about Imam Malik has him answering question after question in one sitting with: I don't know. Whether or not every detail holds, the habit it praises is the one in the verse. Four years of lessons, in the verse's own terms, are a step, not the summit. Someone knows more, and above them, someone more again.
screen: `RAISED BY DEGREES, NEVER AT THE TOP.` · `MUSA SAYS I, THEN WALKS TO LEARN.` · `THE ANGELS: ONLY WHAT YOU TAUGHT US.` · `ALLAH KNOWS BEST. I DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Look for one thing from this year you've talked about as if you were sure, a ruling, a story, a meaning, and you're not. Name it plainly to yourself, I don't actually know this, and let the not-knowing be true for a minute. If you pray, you can add the words Muslims use: Allahu a'lam, Allah knows best.
Humility after learning. The more you learn, the clearer it gets that over every lord of knowledge is one more knowing. Today's word.
Your line: someone knows more. Even a prophet walked a long way to learn. Rest well.

screen: `DAY 1425 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR FOUR CLOSE: THE WAYS.`

1426.title: Year four close: the ways
1426.hook: practice and thought, law and heart, all pointing one direction
1426.howItsDone: Muslims face the qiblah, toward the Kaaba in Mecca, for every prayer, finding it by the mosque's prayer niche, a compass or an app; some also pray voluntary rak'ahs, or bow in a prostration of thanks, when something good happens.

segments.voice: Yesterday: humility after learning, and your line: someone knows more. Today, the last day of year four.

A small arrow is stuck to the ceiling of a hotel room, pointing past the wall, past the parking lot, past everything. A traveler unrolls a mat beneath it. Across town, a family lines up mats in a living room by the compass on a phone. In a mosque, the whole building is already turned that way. Different rooms, different reasons for being there. One direction. This year walked many ways into the faith: practice and thought, law and heart. On its last day, here's where they all point.
screen: `AN ARROW ON A HOTEL CEILING.` → `DIFFERENT ROOMS, ONE DIRECTION.` → `WHERE THE WAYS POINT.`

segments.voice: First, the ways this year took. Practice: the pillars, from the inside. Thought: the creed, and the reports with their careful chains. Law: the schools, standing in one row. Heart: its stations and its diseases, and the manners that show it. Then the life cycle, from the call to prayer in a newborn's ear to the last prayer, and a living ummah across the world. Second, the direction. The Qur'an tells the Prophet, in Pickthall's translation: "So turn thy face toward the Inviolable Place of Worship." That's the qiblah, the Kaaba in Mecca. Every school, every land, every hotel room: one direction in prayer. Third, the direction isn't the whole of it. The same surah says: "It is not righteousness that ye turn your faces to the East and the West." Then it says, in paraphrase, what righteousness is: believing in Allah and the Last Day, giving wealth out of love to family, orphans, the needy and the traveler, keeping the prayer, keeping promises, and patience in hard times. Creed, charity, prayer, manners and heart, in one verse. Fourth, Who the direction is for. Earlier in the same surah: "Unto Allah belong the East and the West, and whithersoever ye turn, there is Allah's Countenance." Muslims face the Kaaba because they were told to, and worship Allah, Who is not held by any building. So the ways of this year aren't rival roads. They're many paths through one life, and in prayer they all turn the same way. Tomorrow, year five: the sources themselves.
screen: `PRACTICE, THOUGHT, LAW, HEART.` · `TURN THY FACE: THE QIBLAH.` · `NOT ONLY EAST OR WEST: RIGHTEOUSNESS.` · `WHEREVER YOU TURN, ALLAH'S COUNTENANCE.`

segments.voice: If you know the direction, turn toward it; if not, simply sit where you are, and let one thing from this year come forward that you're grateful to have met: a verse, a person, a habit that stuck. If you pray, you can give thanks for the year in two voluntary rak'ahs, two units of prayer, with the intention of thanks.

Year four close. The pillars, the reports, the schools, the creed, the heart, the manners, the life cycle, the world, and the gathering of it all: one faith, walked many ways, facing one direction. Today's word.
Your line: all roads face the qiblah. Many ways, one direction. Year four is done, and thank you for walking it.
